title: Comparison sorting: insertion sort vs merge sort
problem_statement: Given a list of n integers, return a new list containing the same elements in non-decreasing order (the input list must not be modified).

input.size_measure: n integers of bounded size; costs are counted in comparisons and element moves, each O(1). The harness draws values uniformly from [-n, n], so duplicates occur.

algorithms.name: insertion sort
algorithms.idea: Grow a sorted prefix one element at a time: shift every larger element of the prefix one place right and drop the new element into the gap.
algorithms.pseudocode: a = copy(xs); for i in 1..n-1: key = a[i]; j = i - 1; while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j+1] = a[j]; j = j - 1; a[j+1] = key; return a
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n + I) where I is the number of inversions: Theta(n^2) in the worst case (reversed input, I = n(n-1)/2) and on average over uniformly random inputs (E[I] = n(n-1)/4 for a random order of distinct elements, and n(n-1)/4 * 2n/(2n+1) for the harness distribution, the case measured for V2; PROOFS.md section 6); Theta(n) on sorted input
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) for the output copy, O(1) extra
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: before iteration i, a[0..i-1] holds the first i input elements in sorted order (Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3; CLRS).

algorithms.name: merge sort
algorithms.idea: Split the list in half, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves in one linear pass.
algorithms.pseudocode: sort(xs): if |xs| <= 1 return copy(xs); L = sort(left half); R = sort(right half); return merge(L, R)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + Theta(n)
algorithms.correctness: Induction on n: merging two sorted lists by repeatedly taking the smaller head yields a sorted list of all their elements (Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3; CLRS).

shape.note: count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

relationship: Insertion sort removes one inversion per element move, and a random list has Theta(n^2) of them in expectation. Merge sort's divide and conquer reaches Theta(n log n), which is optimal for comparison sorting (PROOFS.md section 8).

background.statement: Outside the comparison model, n integers can be sorted in O(n sqrt(log log n)) expected time and linear space (Han and Thorup).

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 3: Sorting and Searching (2nd ed.)

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)
Integer sorting in O(n sqrt(log log n)) expected time and linear space

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with Python's built-in sorted() (used only as the oracle) on random lists from [-n, n], n = 0..5, 8, 16, 50, 100, 500 and 2000; the validator also checks that neither mutates its input. V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): the measured quantity is the exact number of KEY COMPARISONS made by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented key type (CountingKey in harness.py) wrapped around the values of generate() (uniform on [-n, n], the same seeded random inputs the earlier timing fit used, i.e. insertion sort's average case). The instrumentation agrees with a closed form computed from the input alone (insertion sort makes sum over i of g_i + [g_i < i] comparisons, g_i = number of earlier elements larger than a_i) at n = 50, 100, 250, 500. Insertion sort, mean of 3 seeded samples at n = 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000: 15574.67, 63461.67, 250154.67, 999716.33, 3990076 comparisons (0.997 to 1.015 times n^2/4); alpha = 0.999 against n^2. Merge sort, 1 sample (the 3-sample spread was below 0.1% of the count at every n) at n = 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000: 8701, 19408, 42854, 93621, 203198, 438577, 941409 comparisons = n log2 n - c n with c = 1.25 to 1.27; alpha = 1.011 against n log n, the excess coming from the -c n term. Tolerance 0.03 for both: the counts carry no timing noise, so the band only has to cover lower-order terms (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.011) while staying below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: insertion sort against n log n (alpha = 1.743) and n^2 log n (0.931); merge sort against n (1.126), n log^2 n (0.918) and n^2 (0.563). The log factor is therefore resolved for both algorithms (validator diagnostic, RESEARCH_LOG RL-048), which the earlier timing fit at tolerance 0.25 could not do (it would also have passed merge sort against n). Element moves are not counted; experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_sorting.py reproduces every number above. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry from the code (the correctness of both algorithms and the stability of merge sort; insertion sort's Theta(n + I), worst case and exact average case; merge sort's comparison bounds on every input; the Omega(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting in the worst case, on average and for randomized algorithms; the space bounds; the exact counts for all sizes of their domains) and names the scripts and tests that check each one, among them tests/test_proofs_sorting.py.

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(n log n) comparisons: at least log2(n!) = n log2 n - O(n) in the worst case, and also on average over a uniformly random input order, hence in expectation for any randomized comparison sort that is always correct
lower_bounds.setting: comparison model (elements are accessed only through pairwise comparisons)
lower_bounds.source: Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3 (1998), credit; the randomized case follows from the average case by the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle. Own proof of all three cases: PROOFS.md section 8

caveats: The Omega(n log n) lower bound is proved here for the comparison model only; outside it, integers can be sorted faster by exploiting their representation: on the harness range [-n, n], counting sort sorts n integers with O(n) word operations and no element comparison (PROOFS.md section 10; see also background). So merge sort is optimal among comparison sorts, not for integer sorting in general. Insertion sort's cost depends on the input: it is Theta(n + I), linear on sorted lists and on lists with O(n) inversions. V2 measures insertion sort's average case (random input), which is Theta(n^2), the same order as its worst case.
